Being around people in authority or uniform

I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

I have failed in my most important role in life

issues.explanation: Pregnancy/childbirth/babies as a trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile for childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. No memory, threat, or appraisal item links the trauma to pregnancy, childbirth, babies, parenting, or reproductive themes, so this trigger appears clinically disconnected rather than part of a coherent trigger network.

Given the very specific medical cue content, it does not fit well with the otherwise interpersonal/authority-focused profile.

vignette: Amira was seven when her father's hand became an instrument of control. The abuse was not constant, but it was precise: it happened when she stepped out of line, when she spoke back, or when the household grew quiet after his third drink. She remembers the smell of whiskey on his breath mingling with the dust of his study, the sharp crack of his palm against her shoulder, and the way his voice would drop into a flat, unyielding command that brooked no argument. Over the years, Amira had come to believe that the household's stability rested entirely on her ability to anticipate his moods and fulfill his demands without hesitation. When she could not meet his expectations, she felt entirely helpless, certain that no matter how carefully she moved, the worst outcome was always waiting just beyond her control. Now forty-three, Amira works as a pharmacist at a bustling downtown clinic, a role she once viewed as a testament to her diligence. The pharmacy's compounding station has become a place where the past refuses to stay buried. The sharp, chemical tang of isopropyl alcohol rising from the cleaning trays sends a jolt through her chest that makes her step back as though recoiling from a strike. When the lead pharmacist approaches her with a clipboard and directs a sequence of inventory adjustments in a tone that leaves no room for question, her shoulders tighten and her breath shallows. She finds herself bracing for the command to be followed by consequences that never arrive, reacting to the present moment as if the floor might give way beneath her. Her concentration frays during shifts; she will read a prescription label three times and still miss a dosage, her thoughts fracturing into static. At night, Amira lies awake, tracing the contours of the ceiling while her mind holds its breath. She has told herself that staying awake is necessary, that if she drifts off, the past might catch her unguarded. Sleep has become a calculated vigil. During the day, when the memories surface, they do not arrive as quiet reflections. They arrive as full sensory invasions-the weight of his grip, the exact angle of his jaw, the sound of his boots on the hardwood-so vivid and immediate that she must step away from her desk to breathe. When the recall returns, she feels so overwhelmed by the emotion that she has to stop whatever she is doing. Other times, the memory arrives flat and distant, as if she is reading a report about a stranger who lived a life she never recognized. She also presses her thumb into her forearm when the internal tide rises, relying on the physical sting to anchor her attention. These parallel experiences have steadily reshaped Amira's daily rhythm. She watches her colleagues exchange morning pleasantries, noting how their relaxed postures and easy smiles feel entirely foreign to her nervous system. She began declining weekend gatherings when she sensed laughter or optimism in the room, convinced that letting herself feel hopeful would leave her exposed. She stopped pursuing career advancements, telling her husband she was content with her current station. She had come to believe that nothing she constructed held any real meaning, that she was fundamentally incapable of stopping bad things from unfolding. She viewed her current capacity to function as a failure in her most important role as a woman who should be able to build something lasting. The steady presence of these patterns finally brought her to schedule an intake. She is most afraid of losing her composure in front of a supervisor, but beneath that fear lies a fragile, unspoken hope that she might finally learn how to stand in a room without bracing for a blow.
